{{About|the variable selection method|other uses|Counterfeit consumer goods}}
{{short description|Statistical method}}

In [[statistics]], '''the knockoff filter''', or simply '''knockoffs''', is a framework for [[variable selection]]. It was originally introduced for linear regression by [[Rina Barber]] and [[Emmanuel Candès]],<ref name = "Barber 2015">{{cite journal |last1 = Barber | first1 = Rina Foygel | last2 = Candès | first2 = Emmanuel J. |year=2015 |title=Controlling the false discovery rate via knockoffs |journal=Annals of Statistics |volume=43|issue=5 |pages=2055–2085}}</ref> and later generalized to other regression models in the random design setting.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|last1=Candès|first1=Emmanuel|last2=Fan|first2=Yingying|last3=Janson|first3=Lucas|last4=Lv|first4=Jinchi|year=2018|title=Panning for gold: model-X knockoffs for high dimensional controlled variable selection|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society |series=Series B (methodological) |publisher=Wiley Online Library|volume=80|issue=3|pages=551–577|arxiv=1610.02351}}</ref> Knockoffs has found application in many practical areas, notably in [[Genome-wide association study|genome-wide association studies]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Sesia|first=Matteo|last2=Sabatti|first2=Chiara|author2-link=Chiara Sabatti|last3=Candès|first3=Emmanuel|title=Gene hunting with hidden Markov model knockoffs|journal=Biometrika|volume=106|issue=1|pages=1–18|year=2019}}</ref>

== Fixed-X knockoffs ==
Consider a linear regression model with response vector <math>\mathbf y</math> and [[Feature (machine learning)|feature]] matrix <math>\mathbf X</math>, which is treated as deterministic''.'' A matrix <math>\tilde{\mathbf X}</math> is said to be knockoffs of <math>\mathbf X</math> if it does not depend on <math>\mathbf y</math> and satisfies <math>\mathbf X_i^\top\mathbf X_j=\mathbf X_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_j=\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\mathbf X_j=\tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top\tilde{\mathbf X}_j</math> for <math>i\ne j</math>. Barber and Candès showed that, equipped with a suitable feature importance statistic, fixed-X knockoffs can be used for variable selection while controlling the [[false discovery rate]] (FDR).

== Model-X knockoffs ==
Consider a general [[Regression analysis|regression]] model with response vector <math>\mathbf y</math> and random feature matrix <math>\mathbf X</math>''.'' A matrix <math>\tilde{\mathbf X}</math> is said to be knockoffs of <math>\mathbf X</math> if it is [[Conditional independence|conditionally independent]] of <math>\mathbf y</math> given <math>\mathbf X</math> and satisfies a subtle pairwise exchangeable condition: for any <math>j</math>, the joint distribution of the random matrix <math>[\mathbf X,\tilde{\mathbf X}]</math> does not change if its <math>j</math>th and <math>(j+p)</math>th columns are swapped, where <math>p</math> is the number of features. While it is less clear how to create model-X knockoffs compared to their fixed-X counterpart, various [[algorithm]]s have been proposed to construct knockoffs.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bates|first=Stephen|last2=Candès|first2=Emmanuel|last3=Janson|first3=Lucas|last4=Wang|first4=Wenshuo|title=Metropolized knockoff sampling|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|year=2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Huang|first=Dongming|last2=Janson|first2=Lucas|title=Relaxing the assumptions of knockoffs by conditioning|journal=Annals of Statistics|year=2020}}</ref> Once constructed, model-X knockoffs can be used for variable selection following the same procedure as fixed-X knockoffs and control the FDR.

== Properties ==
The knockoffs <math>\tilde{\mathbf X}</math> can be understood as negative controls. Informally speaking, knockoffs has the property that no method can statistically distinguish the original matrix from its knockoffs without looking at <math>\mathbf y</math>. Mathematically, the exchangeability conditions translate to symmetry that allows for an estimation of the [[type I error]] (e.g., if one wishes to choose the FDR as the type I error rate, the false discovery proportion is estimated), which then leads to exact type I error control.

Model-X knockoffs provides valid type I error control regardless of the unknown conditional distribution of <math>\mathbf y</math> given <math>\mathbf X</math>, and it can work with black-box variable importance statistics, including the ones derived from complicated [[machine learning]] methods. A most significant challenge of implementing model-X knockoffs is that it requires nontrivial knowledge on the distribution of <math>\mathbf X</math>, which is usually high-dimensional. This knowledge can be gained with the help of unlabeled data.<ref name=":0" />
